To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the lack of association between macroeconomic growth and child undernutrition in the Indian context is likely due to the fact that the growth did not translate into substantial investments in public developmental spending, nor was it associated with any substantial reduction in poverty.
macroeconomic growth was neither accompanied by increases in public developmental expenditure nor by reductions in aggregate poverty head count ratio in India between 1992-93 and 2005-06.

increases in macroeconomic growth in Indian states have not been associated with substantial increases in public spending on development or reductions in aggregate poverty, and that these factors are also only weakly associated with reductions in child underweight or child stunting.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (i) Does macroeconomic growth in a state translate into substantial investments in public development expenditure that matter for children's nutrition and/or substantially improves incomes of the poor?

there is little evidence to suggest that macroeconomic growth has been associated with substantial reductions in child undernourishment in India.
macroeconomic growth is not a panacea to reduce child undernutrion in India.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the lack of association between increased macro‐economic growth and reduced undernutrition in India could be because macroeconomic growth did not translate into substantial investments in public developmental expenditure that could matter to the nutrition of children, nor did it substantially improve the income of the poor, who are also the most undernourished group in the country.

macroeconomic growth has not translated into substantial investments in developmental spending or reduction of aggregate poverty headcount ratios, which in turn has not translated into any substantial reduction in the prevalence of undernutrition in children.

the inability of growth to translate into improvements in child undernutrition is likely a consequence that growth did not translate into substantial investments in public development expenditure that could improve child nutritional status, nor did it improve incomes of the poorest households, who also have the highest burden of undernutrition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the inability of growth to translate into reducing undernutrition in India can be attributed to the growth not translating into any substantial investments in public development expenditure, which could have mattered for children's nutritional well‐being.
macroeconomic growth has not translated into substantial increases in public spending on development or reduction in aggregate income poverty in India.
a ‘support‐mediated’ rather than a ‘growth‐led’ strategy may be more effective in reducing child undernutrition.
